```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
```

# Goal

We prepare the NHANES 2021-2023 data (dataset 3) for the analyses in Parts 2-4. We follow the steps from
lesson 2 (data exploration, preprocessing, quality control) and answer the guiding questions of Part 1:
structure and variable types, missing values, unusual samples/features, preprocessing, clustering by biology
or by technical factors, and suitability for the next parts.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(ComplexHeatmap)

set.seed(2026)

# parameters: all thresholds in one place
MIN_AGE         <- 20    # adults only
MAX_MISSING     <- 0.50  # remove features that are missing in more than 50% of the analysis population
NZV_SHARE       <- 0.95  # remove features where one value makes up more than 95% of the observations
DUP_COR         <- 0.99  # remove features that correlate more than 0.99 with another feature (same measurement)
SKEW_LIMIT      <- 1     # log2-transform continuous features with skewness above 1
IQR_FACTOR      <- 3     # outlier = more than 3 x IQR outside the quartiles
PCA_MAX_MISSING <- 0.20  # lab features for the PCA may be missing in at most 20% of the participants

nhanes_raw <- read_csv("NHANES_20212023_merged_filtered_1.csv", guess_max = 12000)
# the codebook has a few special characters (e.g. micro sign), hence latin1
codebook <- read_csv("NHANES_20212023_codebook_filtered_1.csv", locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))
```

# Data structure and variable types

```{r structure}
dim(nhanes_raw)
n_distinct(nhanes_raw$SEQN) == nrow(nhanes_raw)   # is SEQN a unique identifier?
codebook %>% count(component)
```

The raw table has **`r nrow(nhanes_raw)` participants** (rows) and **`r ncol(nhanes_raw)` variables**
(columns) from four NHANES components. SEQN is a unique participant identifier.

Almost all columns are stored as numbers, also when they are categories (e.g. `RIAGENDR`: 1 = male, 2 = female).
We therefore assign a variable type using the number of unique values, and we check the categorical ones in the
NHANES documentation.

```{r types}
weights_design <- c("SDDSRVYR", "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU", names(nhanes_raw)[str_starts(names(nhanes_raw), "WT")])

variable_info <- codebook %>%
  filter(variable %in% names(nhanes_raw)) %>%
  mutate(n_unique = map_int(variable, ~ n_distinct(na.omit(nhanes_raw[[.x]]))),
         type = case_when(
           variable == "SEQN"                                ~ "identifier",
           variable %in% weights_design                      ~ "survey weight / design",
           str_detect(label, regex("comment", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "detection limit flag",
           n_unique <= 1                                     ~ "constant",
           n_unique == 2                                     ~ "binary",
           n_unique <= 15                                    ~ "categorical / ordinal / discrete",
           TRUE                                              ~ "continuous"))

variable_info %>% count(type, component) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

```{r types-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(variable_info, aes(x = fct_rev(fct_infreq(type)), fill = component)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "", y = "number of variables", fill = "NHANES component")
```

**Observation.** Most variables are continuous laboratory measurements. A part of the columns are not biological
features: survey weights/design variables and detection-limit flags (a 0/1 code that says whether a value was
below the detection limit). The rule with the number of unique values is a simplification: a few discrete
counts (e.g. household size) end up in the "categorical" group.

# Special codes

NHANES stores "refused" and "don't know" as numbers in the same column as the real answers (e.g. 777 or 999 drinks
per day, or 9 = "don't know" for education). If we leave them, they are treated as real values. We cannot replace
every 7 or 9 by NA, because these are valid values in many columns. So we list the codes per variable (from the
NHANES documentation), only for the variables that are still relevant after filtering.

```{r special-codes}
special_codes <- list(DMDEDUC2 = 9, DMDMARTZ = c(77, 99), ALQ111 = 9, ALQ121 = c(77, 99),
                      ALQ130 = c(777, 999), ALQ142 = c(77, 99), ALQ151 = c(7, 9), DBQ935 = 9,
                      LBXHA = 3, LBXHBC = 3, LBDHEG = 3,      # 3 = indeterminate test result
                      RIDEXPRG = 3, URXPREG = 3)              # 3 = cannot be determined

nhanes <- nhanes_raw
n_recoded <- map_int(names(special_codes), ~ sum(nhanes[[.x]] %in% special_codes[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE))
for (v in names(special_codes)) {
  nhanes[[v]][nhanes[[v]] %in% special_codes[[v]]] <- NA
}
tibble(variable = names(special_codes), n_recoded = n_recoded)
```

Note: some alcohol questions are skipped on purpose (e.g. someone who did not drink in the past year is not asked
how many drinks per day). Those empty values are "not asked" and not a real missing value. We keep this in mind if
we use alcohol variables in Part 2.

# Missing values

## Where are the values missing?

```{r missing-overview, fig.height = 3.5}
missing_per_variable <- tibble(variable = names(nhanes), pct_missing = colMeans(is.na(nhanes)) * 100)

ggplot(missing_per_variable, aes(x = pct_missing)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = "grey40") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "% of participants with a missing value", y = "number of variables")
```

Heatmap of observed (blue) and missing (grey) values for 1000 random participants. Columns are in the order of the
data file (so grouped by NHANES component), rows are split by examination status.

```{r missing-heatmap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6}
heat_rows <- nhanes %>%
  mutate(status = if_else(RIDSTATR == 2, "examined", "interview only")) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1000) %>%
  arrange(status, RIDAGEYR)

heat_vars <- setdiff(names(nhanes), "SEQN")
observed <- 1 * !is.na(as.matrix(heat_rows[, heat_vars]))   # 1 = observed, 0 = missing

Heatmap(observed, name = "value", col = c("0" = "grey90", "1" = "steelblue"),
        heatmap_legend_param = list(at = c(0, 1), labels = c("missing", "observed")),
        cluster_rows = FALSE, cluster_columns = FALSE,
        row_split = heat_rows$status,
        show_row_names = FALSE, show_column_names = FALSE, use_raster = TRUE)
```

## Why are they missing?

* **Interview only** (`RIDSTATR` = 1): `r sum(nhanes$RIDSTATR == 1)` participants were interviewed but did not
  visit the mobile examination centre, so they have no examination or lab data. This is the large grey block.
* **Not eligible**: many measurements only exist for certain ages or sexes (e.g. the alcohol questionnaire for adults,
  pregnancy tests and hormones for women).
* **Subsamples by design**: fasting measurements (glucose, insulin, triglycerides) are only taken in the morning
  session; other panels (e.g. PFAS) only in a random subset of participants.
* **Item non-response**: refusals, failed blood draws, too little sample.

The first three are missing by design: the reason is known and can be predicted from other variables (exam status,
age, sex, session). The fourth type we check below: do participants without a HbA1c result differ from the others?

```{r missing-check}
check <- nhanes %>%
  filter(RIDSTATR == 2, RIDAGEYR >= MIN_AGE) %>%
  mutate(hba1c_missing = is.na(LBXGH))

check %>% group_by(hba1c_missing) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), median_age = median(RIDAGEYR), pct_female = mean(RIAGENDR == 2) * 100,
            median_income_ratio = median(INDFMPIR, na.rm = TRUE))

wilcox.test(RIDAGEYR ~ hba1c_missing, data = check)
chisq.test(table(check$RIAGENDR, check$hba1c_missing))
wilcox.test(INDFMPIR ~ hba1c_missing, data = check)
```

**Interpretation (check this against your output).** Only a small fraction of the examined adults has no HbA1c
value. If the tests show differences in age or income, the missingness is not completely at random (MCAR) but
depends on observed variables (MAR). With such a small fraction the effect on the results is probably limited, but
we mention it as a possible bias.

## What do we do with the missing values?

* Missing by design is handled by **selecting the analysis population** (next section), not by imputation. Imputing
  a pregnancy test for men, or the alcohol questionnaire for children, makes no sense.
* Features that are missing for most participants are **removed** (threshold `r MAX_MISSING * 100`%).
* The remaining item non-response is **not imputed** in this dataset. Each analysis in Parts 2-3 uses the complete
  cases for the variables it needs. In Part 4 we impute only if the algorithm requires it, and we fit the imputation
  on the training data only (to avoid data leakage).

# Analysis population and feature filtering

## Samples

```{r population}
step1 <- nhanes %>% filter(RIDSTATR == 2)                         # examined
step2 <- step1 %>% filter(RIDAGEYR >= MIN_AGE)                    # adults
analysis <- step2 %>% filter(!(RIDEXPRG %in% 1), !(URXPREG %in% 1))  # not pregnant

tibble(step = c("all participants", "examined in the mobile centre", paste0("age >= ", MIN_AGE),
                "not pregnant"),
       n = c(nrow(nhanes), nrow(step1), nrow(step2), nrow(analysis)))
```

We keep examined adults who are not pregnant: only they have lab data, many panels and the education variable are
adult measurements, and pregnancy changes many lab values and the group is too small to study separately.

## Derived variables

Blood pressure was measured three times. We use the mean of the readings instead of the three separate columns.

```{r derived}
analysis <- analysis %>%
  mutate(SBP_mean = rowMeans(across(c(BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3)), na.rm = TRUE),
         DBP_mean = rowMeans(across(c(BPXODI1, BPXODI2, BPXODI3)), na.rm = TRUE),
         across(c(SBP_mean, DBP_mean), ~ if_else(is.nan(.x), NA_real_, .x))) %>%   # all readings missing -> NA
  select(-c(BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3, BPXODI1, BPXODI2, BPXODI3))
```

## Features

We remove, in this order (none of these criteria uses an outcome, so there is no bias towards a research question):

1. detection-limit flags (they are not measurements);
2. features missing in more than `r MAX_MISSING * 100`% of the analysis population;
3. near-zero-variance features: one value in more than `r NZV_SHARE * 100`% of the participants. This also removes
   analytes that are mostly below the detection limit, because NHANES replaces those values by one constant;
4. duplicate measurements: many lab values are reported twice (e.g. mg/dL and mmol/L) and correlate (almost)
   perfectly. Keeping both would count the same information twice.

```{r feature-filter}
flag_vars <- variable_info %>% filter(type == "detection limit flag") %>% pull(variable)
features <- setdiff(names(analysis), c("SEQN", weights_design, flag_vars))
n_start <- length(features)

# 2. too many missing values
features <- features[colMeans(is.na(analysis[features])) <= MAX_MISSING]
n_after_missing <- length(features)

# 3. near-zero variance
top_share <- function(x) { x <- na.omit(x); max(table(x)) / length(x) }
nzv <- features[map_dbl(features, ~ top_share(analysis[[.x]])) > NZV_SHARE]
features <- setdiff(features, nzv)

# 4. duplicates: remove a feature if it correlates > 0.99 with a feature before it in the list
num_features <- features[map_lgl(features, ~ is.numeric(analysis[[.x]]))]
num_features <- num_features[order(str_detect(num_features, "SI$"))]   # SI-unit versions last, so the conventional unit is kept
cor_abs <- abs(cor(analysis[num_features], use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
cor_abs[lower.tri(cor_abs, diag = TRUE)] <- 0
duplicates <- num_features[colSums(cor_abs > DUP_COR, na.rm = TRUE) > 0]
features <- setdiff(features, duplicates)

tibble(step = c("start", "after missing filter", "after near-zero variance", "after removing duplicates"),
       n_features = c(n_start, n_after_missing, n_after_missing - length(nzv), length(features)))

tibble(variable = duplicates) %>% left_join(codebook %>% select(variable, label), by = "variable")
```

```{r keep-columns}
analysis <- analysis %>% select(SEQN, any_of(weights_design), all_of(features))
```

After filtering, **`r length(features)` features** remain for **`r nrow(analysis)` participants**.

## Categorical variables as factors

We give the most important categorical variables readable labels (the others are converted when we use them).

```{r factors}
analysis <- analysis %>%
  mutate(RIAGENDR = factor(RIAGENDR, levels = 1:2, labels = c("male", "female")),
         RIDRETH3 = factor(RIDRETH3),
         DMDEDUC2 = factor(DMDEDUC2, levels = 1:5, ordered = TRUE),
         PHDSESNZ = factor(PHDSESNZ, levels = 0:1, labels = c("morning", "afternoon/evening")),
         RIDEXMON = factor(RIDEXMON, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Nov-Apr", "May-Oct")),
         age_group = cut(RIDAGEYR, breaks = c(19, 39, 59, Inf), labels = c("20-39", "40-59", "60+")))

# continuous features = numeric with more than 15 different values
continuous <- features[map_lgl(features, ~ is.numeric(analysis[[.x]]) && n_distinct(na.omit(analysis[[.x]])) > 15)]
length(continuous)
```

# Distributions and transformation

First a plausibility check of key variables: are there biologically impossible values (data-entry errors)?

```{r plausibility}
analysis %>% select(any_of(c("RIDAGEYR", "BMXBMI", "BMXWAIST", "SBP_mean", "DBP_mean", "LBXGH", "LBXTC", "LBXHGB"))) %>%
  summary()
```

**Interpretation (check this against your output).** The ranges are biologically possible. Extreme but possible
values (e.g. a very high HbA1c in a diabetic) are real and are not removed.

Many lab values are right-skewed: concentrations cannot be negative and a few participants have very high values.
This breaks the assumptions of the linear models and tests of Parts 2-3 and lets a few large values dominate
distance-based methods such as PCA. Continuous features with a skewness above `r SKEW_LIMIT` (and no negative
values) are **log2-transformed**. If a feature contains zeros, we add half of the smallest positive value first.

```{r transform}
skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- na.omit(x)
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}

skew_table <- tibble(variable = continuous,
                     skew_before = map_dbl(continuous, ~ skewness(analysis[[.x]])),
                     min_value = map_dbl(continuous, ~ min(analysis[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE)))

log_vars <- skew_table %>% filter(skew_before > SKEW_LIMIT, min_value >= 0) %>% pull(variable)

analysis_log <- analysis
for (v in log_vars) {
  x <- analysis[[v]]
  offset <- if (min(x, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) min(x[x > 0], na.rm = TRUE) / 2 else 0
  analysis_log[[v]] <- log2(x + offset)
}

skew_table <- skew_table %>%
  mutate(skew_after = map_dbl(variable, ~ skewness(analysis_log[[.x]])))

skew_table %>% filter(variable %in% log_vars) %>% summarise(median_before = median(skew_before),
                                                             median_after = median(skew_after))
```

`r length(log_vars)` of the `r length(continuous)` continuous features were log2-transformed. One unit on the log2
scale is a doubling of the value.

```{r transform-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
example_vars <- intersect(c("LBXHSCRP", "LBXTLG", "LBXSATSI", "LBXIN"), log_vars)

bind_rows(analysis     %>% select(all_of(example_vars)) %>% mutate(scale = "original"),
          analysis_log %>% select(all_of(example_vars)) %>% mutate(scale = "log2")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-scale, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(scale = fct_relevel(scale, "original")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey40") +
  facet_grid(scale ~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "", y = "number of participants")
```

**Normalisation and standardisation.** Normalisation for sequencing depth or library size (lesson 2) does not apply:
NHANES lab values are calibrated concentrations, not counts. Standardisation (z-scores) is **not** applied to the
exported dataset, so that effect sizes stay interpretable. It is only applied inside the heatmap and the PCA below,
so that features with a large numerical range do not dominate.

# Outliers

Outliers are detected with the IQR rule from the lesson, on the log-transformed data. Because we look at many
features, we use a stricter limit (`r IQR_FACTOR` x IQR instead of 1.5 x IQR) so that only extreme values are flagged.

```{r outliers}
is_outlier <- function(x, k = IQR_FACTOR) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- q[2] - q[1]
  x < q[1] - k * iqr | x > q[2] + k * iqr
}

outlier_matrix <- sapply(analysis_log[continuous], is_outlier)     # participants x features (TRUE = outlier)
outliers_per_participant <- rowSums(outlier_matrix, na.rm = TRUE)

# features with the most outliers
tibble(variable = colnames(outlier_matrix), n_outliers = colSums(outlier_matrix, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  left_join(codebook %>% select(variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  arrange(desc(n_outliers)) %>% head(10)
```

```{r outliers-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(tibble(n = outliers_per_participant), aes(x = n)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey40") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "number of extreme values per participant", y = "number of participants")

# which features are extreme in the participant with the most outliers?
top_participant <- which.max(outliers_per_participant)
names(which(outlier_matrix[top_participant, ]))
```

**Interpretation (check this against your output).** Most participants have no extreme value at all. Extreme values
occur mostly in features where they are medically meaningful (e.g. glucose or HbA1c in diabetes, cotinine in smokers).
The participant with the most extreme values has a coherent profile of related features, which points to real
biology and not to random errors. We therefore **keep** all participants, and we store the number of extreme values
per participant (`n_outlying_features`) so that a sensitivity analysis without them remains possible.

# Quality control: do participants cluster by biology or by technical factors?

We use the laboratory features that are missing in at most `r PCA_MAX_MISSING * 100`% of the participants
(the fasting measurements are thereby excluded, as they would limit the analysis to the morning session) and the
participants with complete data on those features. All features are standardised (z-scores).

```{r pca-data}
lab_vars <- codebook %>% filter(component == "Laboratory") %>% pull(variable)
pca_vars <- intersect(continuous, lab_vars)
pca_vars <- pca_vars[colMeans(is.na(analysis_log[pca_vars])) <= PCA_MAX_MISSING]

pca_data <- analysis_log %>% select(SEQN, all_of(pca_vars)) %>% drop_na()
c(n_features = length(pca_vars), n_participants = nrow(pca_data))
```

## Heatmap with hierarchical clustering

200 random participants (columns) and the lab features (rows), both clustered with Ward's method.

```{r heatmap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
hm_sample <- pca_data %>% slice_sample(n = 200)
hm_matrix <- t(scale(hm_sample %>% select(-SEQN)))              # features in rows, scaled per feature
colnames(hm_matrix) <- hm_sample$SEQN
hm_info <- hm_sample %>% select(SEQN) %>%
  left_join(analysis_log %>% select(SEQN, RIAGENDR, age_group, PHDSESNZ), by = "SEQN")

Heatmap(hm_matrix, name = "z-score",
        col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(-3, 0, 3), c("blue", "white", "red")),
        top_annotation = HeatmapAnnotation(sex = hm_info$RIAGENDR, age = hm_info$age_group,
                                           session = hm_info$PHDSESNZ),
        clustering_method_rows = "ward.D2", clustering_method_columns = "ward.D2",
        show_row_names = FALSE, show_column_names = FALSE)
```

## PCA

```{r pca}
pca <- prcomp(pca_data %>% select(-SEQN), center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

explained <- tibble(PC = seq_along(pca$sdev), variance = pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2) * 100)

scores <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:5]) %>%
  mutate(SEQN = pca_data$SEQN) %>%
  left_join(analysis_log %>% select(SEQN, RIAGENDR, RIDAGEYR, age_group, PHDSESNZ, RIDEXMON), by = "SEQN")
```

```{r pca-scree, fig.height = 3.5}
explained %>% filter(PC <= 20) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = variance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "principal component", y = "% of variance explained")
```

```{r pca-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
scores %>%
  pivot_longer(c(RIAGENDR, age_group, PHDSESNZ, RIDEXMON), names_to = "factor", values_to = "level",
               values_transform = list(level = as.character)) %>%
  drop_na(level) %>%
  mutate(factor = recode(factor, RIAGENDR = "sex (biological)", age_group = "age group (biological)",
                         PHDSESNZ = "exam session (technical)", RIDEXMON = "six-month period (technical)")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = level)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", round(explained$variance[1], 1), "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", round(explained$variance[2], 1), "%)"), colour = "")
```

To quantify this, we regress each of the first three PCs on one factor at a time and report the R2 (% of the
variance of the PC explained by that factor).

```{r pca-r2}
r2 <- sapply(c("RIAGENDR", "RIDAGEYR", "PHDSESNZ", "RIDEXMON"), function(v) {
  sapply(paste0("PC", 1:3), function(pc) summary(lm(scores[[pc]] ~ scores[[v]]))$r.squared * 100)
})
round(r2, 1)
```

**Interpretation (check this against your output).** The participants form one continuous cloud, without separate
clusters, as expected in a population sample. The main axes of variation are biological: PC1 is mostly related to
age and PC2 mostly to sex. The technical factors (exam session and six-month period) explain almost none of the
variance. So the participants group by the biology we are interested in, and not by a technical factor, and no batch
correction is needed. Note that the six-month period is linked to geography (the examination centres move with the
season), so even a small association with it is not necessarily a technical artefact.

# Export

The preprocessed dataset contains the analysis population, the retained features (skewed ones on the log2 scale,
same column names), the survey weights and the number of extreme values per participant. There is **no imputation**
and **no standardisation** in the exported file.

```{r export}
final <- analysis_log %>% mutate(n_outlying_features = outliers_per_participant)

variable_dictionary <- tibble(variable = names(final)) %>%
  left_join(codebook %>% select(variable, label, component), by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(log2_transformed = variable %in% log_vars)

dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(final, "output/NHANES_part1_preprocessed.csv")
saveRDS(final, "output/NHANES_part1_preprocessed.rds")      # keeps the factor levels
write_csv(variable_dictionary, "output/NHANES_part1_variable_dictionary.csv")
```

# Summary of the preprocessing decisions

| Step | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Special codes | "refused" / "don't know" / "indeterminate" recoded to NA (list per variable) | these numbers are not real measurements |
| Samples | examined, adult, not pregnant: `r nrow(analysis)` of `r nrow(nhanes)` participants | lab data only for examined participants; adult measurements; pregnancy changes lab values |
| Features | removed flags, > 50% missing, near-zero variance and duplicates: `r length(features)` of `r ncol(nhanes_raw)` columns kept | no information, or the same information twice |
| Missing values | no imputation | missing by design; small item non-response, complete cases per analysis |
| Transformation | log2 for skewness > 1 (`r length(log_vars)` features) | symmetric distributions for models and PCA |
| Standardisation | only inside heatmap and PCA | keep effect sizes interpretable |
| Outliers | extreme values (3 x IQR) flagged, nobody removed | they look like real biology |

# Is the dataset suitable for Parts 2-4?

* **Sample size:** `r nrow(final)` adults and `r length(features)` features is enough for a multivariable
  regression (Part 2), for testing at least 20 features (Part 3) and for a train/test split (Part 4).
* **Covariates:** age, sex, ethnicity, BMI, income-to-poverty ratio and education are available and mostly complete.
* **Fasting variables** (glucose, insulin, triglycerides) only exist for the morning session (about half of the
  participants). Analyses with them use this subsample and must report its size.
* **Log2-transformed variables:** coefficients are per doubling of the value.
* **Limitations:** NHANES is a complex survey (weights and design are not used in our analysis), age and the
  income ratio are top-coded (80+ and 5+), and the data are cross-sectional, so associations are not causal.
